strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how researchers’ collaboration arrangements affect interactive theme discovery. Connecting system evaluation with qualitative research workflows is a worthwhile contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-47hpyj9_/call-15cd9c22dcd140febfdbe793d0960527/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The study compares three substantially different approaches—topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM prompting—through 15 experiments involving 20 researchers. Using a common dataset and fixed initial partitions within each system provides useful experimental control.

The evaluation combines automated measures with a substantial manual audit of 1,200 document–theme pairs, double annotation and adjudication, reported agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha = 0.632), and participant interviews. The appendices supply prompts, initialization settings, and hardware details. These are useful foundations for a reproducible empirical contribution.
weaknesses: The experiment does not implement the central comparison as motivated. Section 1 defines asynchronous collaboration as independent coding followed by joint consolidation, but Section 4 evaluates individual codebooks without consolidation; Section 8 defers consolidation strategies. Consequently, the evidence concerns individuals versus three-person groups. Group size changes alongside collaboration modality, while coding time and total effort are unreported. Participant allocation, randomization, and reuse are also unspecified: the design entails 27 participation slots for 20 people. These omissions prevent a clear attribution of differences to collaboration modality.

The statistical evidence is inadequate for the stated conclusions. Each tool has only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, yielding just one synchronous codebook pair for consistency evaluation. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without specifying observational units or sample sizes. If themes or theme matches are treated as independent observations, dependence within shared codebooks is ignored. Exact p-values, multiplicity handling, and uncertainty at the session level are missing; the 'near statistically significant' designation does not resolve these concerns. The large document collection cannot substitute for independent experimental replication.

The correctness results are insufficiently defined and partly inconsistent with their interpretation. Section 5 describes judging sampled document–theme assignments, whereas Figure 4 reports F1 without explaining the reference labels, recall calculation, or averaging. Uniform sampling across themes also requires clarification of weighting before interpreting results as dataset-wide performance. Confidence intervals are absent. Moreover, the claimed asynchronous correctness advantage for topic modeling is not supported generally by Figure 4: the full-sample scores coincide, and synchronous scores are higher at the middle cumulative thresholds.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger justification. Maximum-similarity theme matching leaves the matching constraints and aggregation across unequal codebooks unclear. Such maxima depend on theme number, size, and granularity, yet resulting theme counts and distributions are not reported. Embedding similarity is also not demonstrated to track meaningful qualitative distinctions. The manual audit evaluates assignment correctness but does not validate the consistency and cohesiveness measures against expert judgments of codebook quality.

Several conclusions exceed the experimental scope. Claims about interaction bandwidth explaining collaboration benefits are hypotheses rather than tested mechanisms. Likewise, one English COVID-19 tweet corpus and one implementation per category cannot establish general properties of entire NLP approaches. The broad conclusions about LLM reliability and scalability rest on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct with a particular prompting configuration; reported runtime alone does not establish comparative efficiency. These claims should be narrowed or supported by additional controlled evidence.

Important reproducibility and qualitative-analysis details remain missing despite Section 9’s assurance of completeness: the exact S-BERT checkpoint, prompt-selection sample sizes and selected templates, generation settings, and treatment of invalid LLM labels in evaluation. The latter matters because Table 4 reports 0.7–16.1% unlabeled documents. Appendix C acknowledges skipped interviews but provides neither interview participation counts nor a systematic analysis procedure, limiting confidence in comparative claims about participant experiences.

The decisive limitation is the soundness and reproducibility of the central empirical comparison. The useful study motivation and descriptive observations do not yet establish a clear Findings contribution. A next-cycle revision could become viable through corrected analysis, complete reporting, and a more tightly scoped or better-controlled collaboration comparison.
